title: Progressive Web Apps Small Examples
description: Use these small Progressive Web Apps examples with the tools described in each lesson. Read the expected result before you try a change.

examples.title: Start with a useful website
examples.description: A progressive web app starts as a working website.
examples.code:
Reading list

Choose a book for today.
examples.output: The page works as a normal website before any app feature is added.

examples.title: Describe the app in a manifest
examples.description: A manifest is a JSON file that describes the app name, start address and display choices.
examples.output: Save this as manifest.webmanifest. It supplies app details; a browser may need valid icons and other checks before offering installation.

examples.title: Link the manifest and icons
examples.description: The page must link its manifest. Icons should be real image files in the sizes declared by the manifest.
examples.code:
<link rel="manifest" href="/manifest.webmanifest">
<meta name="theme-color" content="#174a8b">
<!-- In the manifest, add real 192x192 and 512x512 PNG icons with their actual sizes. -->
examples.output: The browser can discover the manifest from the page. In its app tools, check that the manifest and icons load without errors.

examples.title: Register a service worker
examples.description: A service worker is a script that the browser can run separately from the page.
examples.output: On HTTPS or localhost, the browser tries to install sw.js. Put an actual worker file at that path.

examples.title: Install an offline page
examples.description: The install event is a chance to prepare files for later use.
examples.output: The worker stores a real offline.html page in the named cache during installation.

examples.title: Give navigation an offline fallback
examples.description: A fetch handler can try the network first and use a saved page when that request fails.
examples.output: Page navigation uses the network when available. If it fails, a cached offline page or a plain message is returned.

examples.title: Choose a cache rule for a purpose
examples.description: Cache-first uses a stored response before trying the network.
examples.output: The helper reuses a stored response. On a first successful fetch, it saves a copy and returns the original response.

examples.title: Remove your own old caches
examples.description: The activate event can tidy old cache versions.
examples.output: Old reading-prefixed caches are removed. The two current names are kept.

examples.title: Understand a waiting update
examples.description: A new worker may wait while the old one still controls open pages.
examples.output: The console shows the active worker and, when present, a waiting version. The values depend on the current installation state.

examples.title: Save a small local preference
examples.description: A page can remember a small choice in localStorage.
examples.output: On a page where storage is allowed, the console shows dark. The catch handles blocked or unavailable storage.

examples.title: Treat network hints as hints
examples.description: The online and offline events are useful clues.
examples.code:
window.addEventListener("offline", () => console.log("The browser reports offline."));
window.addEventListener("online", () => console.log("The browser reports online. Try the request again."));
examples.output: The page can explain a change in connection state. It still needs to catch failures from each real request.

examples.title: Test and reset your practice app
examples.description: A PWA needs tests for first visit, repeat visit, offline use and updates.
examples.code:
Open Application tools on your own local project.
Check manifest errors and worker scope.
Load once online, then test offline navigation.
Change sw.js and inspect the waiting version.
For a clean test, unregister only your practice worker and clear only its app caches.
examples.output: These checks show whether the fallback, scope and update behaviour match your design.
